rows: Before the NBA, Wilt toured the Soviet Union with the Globetrotters and shook Khrushchev’s hand.
Wilt’s warm-up act: a Globetrotters season, a trip to Moscow, a handshake with Khrushchev.

Before his NBA debut, Wilt Chamberlain spent a full season with the Harlem Globetrotters. Their 1959 Soviet tour took him to Moscow, where he shook hands with Nikita Khrushchev. The Globetrotters were more than a brief stop on his way to the NBA: their official history records that he returned to play with them during several NBA offseasons.
Bill Russell high-jumped too: in 1956 he tied a future Olympic high-jump champ at a meet.
1956: Russell matched a future Olympic high-jump champion. Then he won Olympic gold in hoops.

Bill Russell was competing against elite high jumpers while becoming a basketball champion. At the 1956 West Coast Relays, he cleared 6 feet, 9¼ inches, tying Charlie Dumas, who would win Olympic high-jump gold later that year. Russell’s own Olympic gold came in basketball. His university remembers him as the world’s seventh-ranked high jumper in 1956.
Kareem writes mysteries: his novels star Sherlock Holmes’s smarter brother, Mycroft.
Kareem read Sherlock Holmes as a rookie. Decades later he wrote Mycroft Holmes novels.

Kareem Abdul-Jabbar recalled receiving a two-volume collection of Sherlock Holmes stories during his rookie NBA season in Milwaukee. He read it on buses and in the locker room. Decades later, the basketball star became a Holmes author himself: he and Anna Waterhouse co-wrote the 2015 novel Mycroft Holmes, building a mystery around Sherlock’s older brother.
The rookie who became a mystery novelist
When Jerry West won a state title, his hometown put up a sign calling itself “West Bank.”
Jerry West’s hometown celebrated his 1956 state title with a “West Bank” sign. Unofficial, but loud.

After Jerry West scored 39 points to help East Bank win its first state basketball title in March 1956, the hometown celebration reached the city-limits sign. A contemporary newspaper reported a temporary proclamation of “West Bank.” It also explicitly explained that the town had not officially changed its name. The tribute was exuberant hometown wordplay, not a municipal renaming.
When East Bank became West Bank
1961–62: Elgin Baylor played Lakers games on Army weekend passes. Still averaged 38.
Baylor was stationed at Fort Lewis and flew in on weekends. 48 games, about 38 points a night.

During the 1961–62 season, Elgin Baylor was on active Army duty at Fort Lewis, Washington. Weekend liberty allowed him to fly or drive to Lakers games, fitting an NBA season around military service. He appeared in only 48 games, yet scored more than 1,800 points, averaging about 38 a night. His extraordinary season was also an extraordinary commute.
The soldier on weekend basketball duty
Bob Cousy went to Boston out of a hat. His first Celtics contract talk was in a bathroom, he says.
Nobody wanted Cousy, so his name went in a hat. Boston drew him. Six rings later, nobody complains.

Bob Cousy remembered his first Celtics contract negotiation taking place in a men’s room because Walter Brown’s office was occupied. The route there had already been peculiar: after the Chicago Stags folded, Boston acquired him through a drawing from a hat. Cousy said he asked Brown for $10,000 and settled for $9,000, with the bathroom serving as an improvised negotiating room.
Cousy’s contract talks in the men’s room
1950: Fort Wayne just held the ball against Mikan’s Lakers and won 19–18. No shot clock yet.
The lowest-scoring game in NBA history, 19–18, was a plan to keep the ball away from George Mikan.

To beat George Mikan’s Lakers in November 1950, Fort Wayne tried keeping the ball away from him almost entirely. With no shot clock, the Pistons could stall rather than challenge the dominant center. The Lakers fouled to regain possession, but Fort Wayne won 19–18. That was the final score, not a quarter. The NBA’s shot clock arrived four years later.
1968, the Astrodome: Elvin Hayes put up 39 and ended UCLA’s 47-game winning streak.
A 60% free-throw shooter, Elvin Hayes hit the two that beat UCLA in the 1968 Game of the Century.

In January 1968, Elvin Hayes faced UCLA before 52,693 people inside Houston’s Astrodome. The basketball court had been brought in from Los Angeles. Hayes, shooting about 60 percent at the foul line that season, made two free throws with 28 seconds left. Houston won 71–69, ending UCLA’s 47-game winning streak. Hayes finished the stadium-sized showdown with 39 points.
Two free throws inside the Astrodome
Nate Thurmond ran a barbecue place in San Francisco. The sauce was his mom’s recipe.
After the NBA, Big Nate’s BBQ: ribs, his mother’s sauce and Warriors talk with Nate himself.

Nate Thurmond spent two decades running Big Nate’s barbecue in San Francisco. Fans could find him descending the spiral stairs from his office to talk Warriors. The sauce used his mother’s recipe. He later explained that he sold the restaurant after tiring of the smoke.
Sweetwater Clifton is also in the 16-inch softball Hall of Fame. He fielded barehanded.
Nat “Sweetwater” Clifton: Knicks big man, Globetrotter, and Hall of Fame softball player.

Nat “Sweetwater” Clifton earned a place in a second sporting world: Chicago’s 16-inch softball, played without gloves. A left-handed power hitter and first baseman for teams including the Brown Bombers, he was honored by that sport’s Hall of Fame. His basketball enshrinement came in 2014, but his unusual sporting résumé already included barehanded fielding and a much bigger ball.
Oscar’s Crispus Attucks won the 1955 Indiana title: the first all-Black school to win a state crown.
Oscar’s champions got one lap downtown, then were sent back to their neighborhood. They won again in ’56.

Oscar Robertson helped Indianapolis’s all-Black Crispus Attucks team win Indiana’s 1955 basketball championship and repeat undefeated in 1956. Yet the victors did not receive the usual extended downtown celebration. Indiana’s Historical Bureau records that each year the team’s firetruck made only one lap around Monument Circle before returning to its neighborhood. The championships and those unequal celebrations belonged to the same segregated city.
The champions with the shortened parade
Joe Fulks learned to shoot with tin cans and bits of brick until a coach gave him a real ball.
One of the first great jump shooters started out throwing cans at a hoop in Kentucky.

A 1948 Sport magazine profile described Joe Fulks practicing after older boys left the local court. Without a basketball, the youngster shot tin cans and pieces of brick, damaging the nets. Coach Luther Goheen discovered what was happening and gave him an old ball. The boy improvising with scrap eventually became a professional scoring champion and helped Philadelphia win the 1947 title.
The tin-can shooter who needed a basketball
Dolph Schayes broke his right wrist, played in a cast, and came back with a deadly left hand.
A cast on his shooting hand forced Dolph Schayes to go lefty. He kept both.

Dolph Schayes played through a broken right wrist with a lightweight cast that left his fingers exposed. In a later interview, he explained that he could still catch the ball and take two-handed set shots. A 1953 profile recorded another consequence: Schayes said playing with the cast had forced him to develop his left hand. An injury had changed his basketball toolkit.
The cast that left his fingers free
Paul Arizin didn’t make his high school team. Villanova found him already enrolled there.
Villanova’s coach tried to recruit Paul Arizin from a local league. He was already a Villanova student.

Villanova’s account of discovering Paul Arizin has an unusual punch line. He impressed coach Al Severance while playing for an independent team against a squad made up of Villanova players. When Severance approached him about attending college, Arizin was already a Villanova freshman. The future star had reached campus without joining the basketball team; the coach found him playing elsewhere.
The recruit who was already enrolled
George Yardley was the first NBA player to score 2,000 in a season. Day job later: Stanford engineer.
Yardley studied engineering at Stanford and ran his own engineering firm after basketball.

George Yardley retired from the NBA in 1960 and put his Stanford civil-engineering education to work. According to the university’s magazine, he founded a business representing engineered products and patented a seal for a rocket’s liquid-oxygen tank. Basketball had made him famous, but his next career involved industrial equipment and a piece of hardware designed for rockets.
From NBA star to rocket hardware
Bob Pettit was cut as a high school sophomore. A backyard hoop later, he was a state champ.
Cut in high school, Bob Pettit practised alone at home. He became the first NBA MVP.

Bob Pettit was cut from his high-school basketball team as a sophomore. His father put up a backyard hoop, and Pettit worked on his game until he returned as a starter the next year. By his senior season, he helped Baton Rouge High win the state championship. The eventual NBA great’s early ambition, he later recalled, was simply to earn a varsity letter.
The cut sophomore in the backyard
Neil Johnston won three straight scoring titles, then coached rookie Wilt Chamberlain.
Neil Johnston pitched in the Phillies’ minor leagues before he became an NBA scoring champ.

Neil Johnston’s professional path began with a Philadelphia Phillies baseball contract after two years at Ohio State. He ultimately switched to basketball and joined the Philadelphia Warriors in 1951, becoming a three-time NBA scoring champion. His connection to another legendary scorer came later: after retiring as a player, Johnston coached the Warriors during Wilt Chamberlain’s first two NBA seasons.
A Phillies contract before NBA scoring titles
Valentine’s Day 1990: Jordan’s jersey was stolen in Orlando. He wore a nameless No. 12 and scored 49.
MJ once played in No. 12, no name on the back. Somebody had swiped his 23 in Orlando.

Michael Jordan arrived in Orlando on Valentine's Day 1990 with a problem: his usual No. 23 jersey had disappeared. Chicago had no suitable replacement, so he played in a nameless No. 12. The unfamiliar uniform did little to disguise him. Jordan scored 49 points, yet Orlando still won 135–129 in overtime. For one night, the most recognizable basketball player in the world had no name on his back.
1986 vs Portland: Bird shot lefty a lot of the night. 47 points, a triple-double.
Bird went left-handed for fun against Portland and dropped 47. Saving the right for the Lakers, he said.

In Portland on February 14, 1986, Larry Bird started finishing shots with his left hand. The famous 'left-handed game' still included ordinary right-handed jumpers, but Bird piled up 47 points, 14 rebounds and 11 assists. He also hit the overtime winner in Boston's 120–119 victory. Asked about his unusual approach, he joked that he was saving his right hand for the Lakers, Boston's next opponent.
The left-handed game that was not all left-handed
Magic and Bird became friends over lunch at Bird’s mom’s house, shooting a Converse ad in 1985.
The rivalry thawed over lunch in French Lick. Magic says he left a Bird friend.

Magic Johnson and Larry Bird barely spoke when they arrived for a 1985 Converse commercial in Bird's hometown of French Lick. In a joint NPR interview years later, Johnson recalled being nervous around his rival. Then they ate lunch at Bird's house. Bird's mother welcomed Johnson, and the players discovered shared Midwestern roots and priorities. Johnson said the encounter changed his view of Bird. Their basketball rivalry survived; their personal relationship had changed.
The commercial lunch that changed a rivalry
Mother’s Day 1987: Isiah played a playoff game while his mom walked at his IU graduation for him.
Isiah promised his mom a degree. She walked for him at Indiana while he played the playoffs.

Isiah Thomas left Indiana for the NBA with a promise to his mother: he would finish college. He kept taking summer classes. On Mother's Day in 1987, basketball and commencement collided. While Thomas made the winning basket against Atlanta in the playoffs, Mary Thomas wore his cap and gown at Indiana's ceremony. He later said seeing his mother represent him meant more than making the shot. He completed his degree that year.
His mother walked while he hit the winner
Barkley says he ate his way up the scale to scare off the Sixers before the 1984 draft. They took him anyway.
Philly picked Barkley fifth in 1984, extra pounds and all.

Charles Barkley says he tried to make Philadelphia pass on him in the 1984 draft by deliberately gaining weight. In a Sports Illustrated interview, he recalled first meeting the Sixers' weight target, then learning they could initially offer far less money than he expected. He responded with a spree of oversized restaurant meals before his next weigh-in. The plan failed: Philadelphia selected him fifth anyway.
Trying to eat his way out of the draft
Hakeem has an official quadruple-double, 1990 vs Milwaukee. A stat review erased another weeks earlier.
Points, rebounds, assists and blocks in double digits: Hakeem did it in 1990. Almost twice.

In March 1990, Hakeem Olajuwon briefly appeared to have a quadruple-double against Golden State. An assist added after the game was rejected by the NBA, leaving him one short. Twenty-six days later, he produced an official one against Milwaukee: 18 points, 16 rebounds, 10 assists and 11 blocks. The same month delivered both a statistical near-miss and the genuine rarity that no scoring review could erase.
The quadruple-double he had to do again
David Robinson grew too tall for Navy ships, so his service was cut to two years. The Spurs waited.
The Admiral was a real Naval Academy grad. San Antonio drafted him and waited two years.

David Robinson's growth spurt became a federal paperwork problem. He entered the Naval Academy with a height waiver, then grew still taller, raising questions about sea duty and commissioning. After he became the NBA's first draft pick in 1987, his active-duty obligation was reduced from five years to two. A federal audit examined the decision, documenting confused expectations and a compromise between Robinson and the Navy. His unusual basketball route came with its own General Accounting Office report.
The draft pick with a federal paper trail
Ewing’s jersey hangs in the Garden. Security still kept asking him for a pass, he joked.
Patrick Ewing, No. 33 in the rafters, getting carded at Madison Square Garden. True story, he says.

Patrick Ewing returned to Madison Square Garden in 2021 as Georgetown's coach and found himself repeatedly being asked for credentials. After a Big East tournament win, he told reporters that security kept stopping him. The former Knicks star joked about checking whether his retired jersey was still hanging above the court. The arena responded that he was a beloved member of its family. Even a familiar face can have a surprisingly awkward homecoming.
Asked for a pass beneath his own retired jersey
1996: Rodman arrived at his own book signing in a wedding dress, by horse-drawn carriage.
Dennis Rodman once married himself for a book launch. Gown, carriage, the works.

Dennis Rodman promised a wedding, then arrived in Manhattan in a horse-drawn carriage wearing a white bridal gown, veil and blond wig. Four women in tuxedos accompanied him. The destination on August 21, 1996, was a Barnes & Noble signing for his book, Bad As I Wanna Be. Crowds stretched along the street. The elaborate bridal entrance was a publicity event for an autobiography, not evidence of a legal marriage to himself.
The bridal procession to a book signing
Scottie Pippen started college as the team manager. He left as the No. 5 pick.
Central Arkansas walk-on and team manager to Hall of Famer. Pippen grew into it, literally.

Scottie Pippen arrived at Central Arkansas without a basketball scholarship and began as a walk-on and team manager. A scholarship opened during his freshman year. Then the lightly recruited guard kept growing into a much taller player without losing his ball skills. By 1987, he was the fifth NBA draft pick, with his rights traded to Chicago. One of basketball's most unlikely development stories began with a job helping run the college team.
From team manager to lottery pick
Gary Payton got “The Glove” from his cousin: he held scorers like a mitt holds a baseball.
Payton says he didn’t even realise “The Glove” meant him at first.

Gary Payton's famous nickname initially confused Gary Payton. In a 2013 interview, he said his cousin started calling him The Glove in 1993, and he did not immediately realize whom the cousin meant. The comparison was to a baseball glove: a ball caught inside could not get out. Payton loved the description of his defense, and an offhand family nickname became the label attached to his entire basketball identity.
The Glove did not recognize his own nickname
Shawn Kemp’s famous point after dunking on Alton Lister? Payback for an earlier scuffle, he says.
Kemp dunked on Alton Lister in 1992 and pointed at him. One of the great poster moments.

Shawn Kemp's 1992 dunk over Alton Lister became famous for the crouching, double-point celebration afterward. Kemp later offered a peculiar footnote: he said some of his frustration was aimed at the wrong person. He had believed Lister grabbed him during an earlier altercation, but later realized it was Tim Hardaway. Lister has also recalled that mix-up. The dunk was real; the grievance behind its most theatrical flourish involved mistaken identity.
The revenge dunk aimed at the wrong grievance
At the 1992 Olympics, Stockton chatted with American fans in Barcelona. Nobody knew he was on the Dream Team.
John Stockton: Dream Teamer, all-time assists leader, and totally unrecognised in Barcelona.

At the 1992 Olympics, John Stockton could walk through Barcelona with a freedom many of his Dream Team teammates lacked. Documentary footage shows him approaching American visitors and asking whether they were watching the team, without being recognized as one of its players. A contemporary report also described him going unrecognized by a woman wearing a Dream Team shirt. One of basketball's elite players could still have an anonymous conversation about basketball.
The Dream Teamer who could interview the fans
After the 1998 Finals, Karl Malone wrestled Dennis Rodman at WCW Bash at the Beach.
The Mailman tag-teamed with Diamond Dallas Page against Rodman and Hulk Hogan. Pro wrestling, 1998.

Karl Malone and Dennis Rodman faced each other in the 1998 NBA Finals, then took their rivalry to a completely different stage. At WCW's Bash at the Beach that summer, Malone teamed with Diamond Dallas Page against Rodman and Hulk Hogan. Two NBA stars were now part of a professional-wrestling tag match. The crossover turned a familiar basketball matchup into an arena spectacle with partners, costumes and an entirely different rulebook.
From the NBA Finals to a wrestling tag team
Reggie came home bragging about 39 points. His sister Cheryl had scored 105 that night.
Reggie Miller wasn’t even the best shooter in his house. Cheryl Miller once scored 105 in a game.

Reggie Miller remembered coming home proud of a 39-point high-school game, only to discover that his sister Cheryl had scored 105 the same evening. His future NBA scoring feats could not help him win that particular family comparison. The anecdote appears in his own memoir and in later biographies; Cheryl has also recalled his excited arrival and surprise. The Miller household had an unusually demanding standard for what counted as a big night.
A great scoring night, second place at home
Mutombo went to Georgetown hoping to become a doctor. He built a hospital in Kinshasa instead.
Finger wag on the court, a hospital in his hometown off it. Dikembe Mutombo.

Dikembe Mutombo came to Georgetown on an academic scholarship intending to pursue medicine and help people back home. Basketball changed his career, but not that larger ambition. After becoming an NBA star, he established a foundation and helped build a hospital in Kinshasa, named for his mother, Biamba Marie Mutombo. It opened in 2007. His original plan had been to return as a doctor; his basketball career instead helped create a place where doctors could work.
The would-be doctor who built a hospital
Muggsy’s real name is Tyrone. Some of his teammates never knew.
Muggsy Bogues hated the nickname at first. Now it’s the only name anyone knows.

Muggsy Bogues says his family first called him Apple because his closely cropped head looked shiny. A childhood friend later supplied Muggsy, inspired by a character in The Bowery Boys. Bogues initially disliked it, thinking it was an insult before he had even seen the show. Eventually he embraced it so completely that, in his own account, some NBA teammates did not know his real first name was Tyrone.
The Microwave turned a pallet business into Piston Group, a major auto-parts supplier.
Vinnie Johnson won two titles in Detroit, then built a car-parts company there.

Vinnie Johnson's second career kept him connected to Detroit in an unexpected way. After winning two championships with the Pistons, he founded Piston Automotive in the mid-1990s. The business began with corrugated pallets and expanded into automotive assembly, supplying major carmakers. His own company biography describes creating opportunities for Detroit residents as a founding aim. The former basketball Piston had become part of the Motor City's actual manufacturing economy.
From the Detroit Pistons to Piston Automotive
Mark Eaton was fixing cars when a coach talked him into basketball. He became a two-time DPOY.
A 7′4″ auto mechanic got recruited off the shop floor. Mark Eaton led the NBA in blocks four times.

Before Mark Eaton became an NBA center, he was working as an auto mechanic. Cypress College recounts that assistant basketball coach Tom Lubin noticed him while visiting the shop, looking through the window of a car raised on a lift. Lubin kept encouraging the unusually tall mechanic to try college basketball. Eaton eventually did, beginning a route through Cypress and UCLA to Utah. His recruiting breakthrough happened beside a car, rather than on a basketball court.
The NBA prospect discovered at an auto shop
Kobe won an Oscar: “Dear Basketball,” his retirement poem turned short film, 2018.
Five rings, two Finals MVPs and an Academy Award. Kobe’s “Dear Basketball.”

Kobe Bryant announced his retirement with a poem. Then he turned that farewell into an animated film, joining forces with veteran animator Glen Keane and composer John Williams. Bryant narrated the story himself, tracing a basketball life from childhood dreams to the Lakers. In 2018, Dear Basketball won the Academy Award for best animated short. His goodbye to one career had become a trophy in another.
The retirement note that became an Oscar
Shaq Diesel, Shaq’s 1993 rap album, went platinum.
Shaq the rapper sold a million records. His producer says he hung up on him at first.

When Shaquille O’Neal called rapper Chip Fu about making an album, the first call went nowhere. In an oral history, Chip Fu recalled hanging up because prank callers had already impersonated Shaq. A second call convinced him, and soon the enormous center was visiting his family’s Brooklyn home to work on music. Their collaboration became part of Shaq Diesel, the 1993 debut that sold more than a million copies.
The phone call that sounded fake
At Wake Forest, Tim Duncan co-wrote a psychology chapter. Title: “Blowhards, Snobs, and Narcissists.”
The Big Fundamental majored in psychology and has a published chapter on egotism.

Tim Duncan’s name appears in a place few basketball fans would search: a psychology book’s table of contents. While he was a Wake Forest undergraduate, he helped write a chapter on why excessive egotism gets under people’s skin. Published in 1997, it was titled Blowhards, Snobs, and Narcissists. The future NBA star shared the byline with three other researchers studying how people respond to self-important behavior.
The academic chapter about annoying people
KG played himself in Uncut Gems, and says he got lost rewatching his old playoff games for it.
Kevin Garnett, movie star: Uncut Gems, 2019, as himself.

Kevin Garnett revisited his own career for Uncut Gems. The 2019 film cast him as a fictional version of himself during Boston’s 2012 playoffs. Garnett recalled that he and the filmmakers became absorbed in those old games, even though everyone already knew the results, sometimes forgetting they were making a movie.
Rewatching his own past on set
Dirk’s mentor trained him with physics books and musical instruments alongside the jumper.
Holger Geschwindner built Dirk’s shot with math, and made him read and play music too.

Dirk Nowitzki’s basketball education came with unusually broad homework. In a German radio interview, he recalled meeting mentor Holger Geschwindner at fifteen. Alongside shooting and movement lessons, Geschwindner handed him physics books and musical instruments. Nowitzki described a teacher who pushed him beyond the court and wanted to develop him as a person. Training the future scoring star included things that would never appear in a box score.
The shooting coach who assigned physics
Steve Nash helped light the Olympic cauldron at the 2010 Vancouver Winter Games.
Two-time MVP, Olympic torchbearer: Nash lit the cauldron in Vancouver in 2010.

At Vancouver’s 2010 Winter Olympics, one of the people chosen to light the cauldron was a basketball player. Steve Nash joined Wayne Gretzky, Nancy Greene Raine and Catriona Le May Doan for the opening-ceremony moment. The ceremony then hit a mechanical snag: Le May Doan’s section failed to work, preventing her from lighting it. She finally got that opportunity at the closing ceremony, giving the unusual torch-lighting story a second ending.
A point guard at the Winter Games
Iverson won state titles in football AND basketball in the same school year at Bethel High.
AI was a star quarterback too: Bethel High, 1992–93, two state championships.

Allen Iverson’s biggest school year came with two very different playbooks. At Bethel High in Virginia, he played quarterback, returned punts and defended passes on the football team that won a state championship in 1992. The following spring, he helped the basketball team win a state title too. Decades later, Bethel retired his football jersey, giving a second sport its own ceremony to celebrate a player mostly remembered for basketball.
Ray Allen starred as Jesus Shuttlesworth in Spike Lee’s “He Got Game.”
Spike Lee spotted Ray Allen at the Garden and cast him as the lead in He Got Game.

Ray Allen’s route to a movie lead began during a road game. In his account, Spike Lee watched him play at Madison Square Garden in March 1997, then approached him about auditioning for He Got Game. Allen was an NBA rookie with no acting experience. The courtside conversation eventually put him opposite Denzel Washington as Jesus Shuttlesworth, a fictional basketball prodigy portrayed by an actual NBA guard.
Shaq named him: “Paul Pierce is the truth.” That was after Pierce dropped 42 on the Lakers.
The Truth got his nickname from Shaquille O’Neal, 2001.

Paul Pierce left a 2001 game against the Lakers with a loss and something more durable: a nickname. He had scored 42 points, making 13 of 19 shots, in Boston’s 112–107 defeat. Afterward, Shaquille O’Neal summoned a Boston reporter and praised Pierce as the Truth. An opponent’s postgame assessment became the label that followed Pierce through the rest of his basketball life.
The nickname awarded by an opponent
Game 7 day, 2001: Vince walked at his UNC graduation, flew to Philly, took the last shot that night.
Vince Carter went to graduation the morning of a Game 7. The final shot rimmed out.

Vince Carter squeezed two major occasions into May 20, 2001. He attended North Carolina’s graduation in a blue gown, left roughly twenty minutes into the ceremony, and flew to Philadelphia for Toronto’s Game 7. That afternoon he had a chance to win the series at the buzzer, but his jumper missed. One day had taken him from a university celebration to a season-ending playoff shot, with an airplane trip in between.
T-Mac pitched pro baseball for the Sugar Land Skeeters in 2014.
After the NBA, Tracy McGrady tried pitching. Sugar Land Skeeters, independent league, 2014.

Tracy McGrady’s retirement detour eventually earned him a baseball bobblehead. In 2014, he joined the Sugar Land Skeeters and made four starts as a pitcher in the independent Atlantic League. He also started that league’s All-Star Game. Four years later, Sugar Land welcomed him back for a ceremonial first pitch and a bobblehead night, commemorating the brief baseball chapter in a career famous for basketball.
The baseball bobblehead for an NBA star
As Nets coach, Jason Kidd spilled a drink on purpose to stop play. NBA fine: $50,000.
Kidd’s “accidental” soda spill cost him $50,000. The NBA ruled it wasn’t an accident.

Jason Kidd’s first season coaching Brooklyn produced an expensive courtside spill. With 8.3 seconds left against the Lakers on November 27, 2013, a drink hit the floor and delayed the game. The NBA ruled that Kidd had spilled it intentionally and fined him $50,000 the next day. Brooklyn still lost 99–94, leaving a small puddle with a remarkably large price tag.
Steve Francis says he practised jumpers through the open top of a phone booth as a kid.
Stevie Franchise sharpened his shot on a phone booth: tiny opening, no room for error.

Steve Francis described an unusual childhood shooting target: a phone booth with its roof removed. In his recollection, the square opening barely admitted a basketball, so a shot needed a precise, high arc. He practiced crossovers and step-back jumpers into that tiny target, hearing the ball rattle against the booth. Long before NBA arenas, one of his practice baskets had originally been built for making calls.
The phone booth with a jump shot
Rasheed Wallace played exactly one game for Atlanta in 2004. Then Detroit, and a title.
One game as a Hawk, then a ring with the Pistons. Rasheed’s 2004 was a ride.

Rasheed Wallace’s Atlanta career fit into a single evening. Acquired from Portland in February 2004, he played one game for the Hawks, scoring 20 points with six rebounds and five blocks against New Jersey. Ten days after his arrival, another trade sent him to Detroit. By June, he was a champion with the Pistons, leaving that lone Hawks appearance as a strange connecting flight in a title-winning season.
Ben Wallace’s big brothers made him chase rebounds on the family team. It stuck.
Undrafted Ben Wallace became a four-time DPOY. It started chasing rebounds for his brothers.

Ben Wallace recalled getting interested in organized basketball because his brother came home with a pile of thrift-store uniforms. They carried the unfamiliar name Eastern Exchange, but they were enough to outfit a makeshift community team. Wallace wanted a jersey and a chance to play with his brothers. He said they expected him to chase rebounds, an early role that sounds especially fitting when told by a future defensive great.
The thrift-store jerseys that started it
Billups and KG bonded during airport delays after the 1995 McDonald’s All-American game.
Chauncey Billups met Kevin Garnett at an airport in 1995. Years later they were teammates.

Chauncey Billups recalled that a pair of delayed flights helped turn Kevin Garnett into a lifelong friend. After the 1995 McDonald’s All-American Game, they spent hours in an airport talking about basketball and their futures. Years later, when Billups’s NBA career needed a reset, he joined Garnett in Minnesota. An interruption to the teenagers’ travel plans had helped build a relationship that followed them into professional basketball.
The friendship formed during a flight delay
Chris Webber collects Black history artifacts and documents and shows them to kids.
C-Webb’s other passion: a collection of Black history, from letters to famous objects.

Chris Webber’s collection included a James Brown suit. In a 2020 interview, he recalled buying it at his charity auction and owning Brown’s handwritten song Staying Power. He used historical items when speaking to children, explaining that even a famous person’s messy handwriting could make greatness feel reachable.
James Brown’s suit in his collection
2003 three-point contest: the buzzer went early on Peja. He got a redo and won it again.
Peja Stojaković won back-to-back three-point contests, the second after a clock glitch and a redo.

Peja Stojaković had to deal with an opponent no shooting drill prepares you for: an early buzzer. During the 2003 three-point contest final, the horn sounded while he was only partway through the racks. He received a do-over and went on to defeat Wesley Person, defending his title. Person had also been his final-round opponent the previous year, so even the rematch needed a restart.
The three-point contest that needed a do-over
Barkley said Yao couldn’t score 19 in a game. Yao scored 20. Barkley kissed a donkey on TV.
Yao Ming’s 20 points cost Charles Barkley a smooch with a donkey. 2002.

Yao Ming made nine shots without a miss against the Lakers in November 2002, finishing with 20 points. That was enough to wreck Charles Barkley’s prediction that the rookie would not score 19 in a game. Barkley had attached an embarrassing promise involving Kenny Smith’s backside. TNT found a comic substitute: a rented donkey marked Kenny’s. A few days after Yao’s breakthrough, Barkley paid up on television with a kiss.
Amar’e soaked in red wine baths. He doesn’t drink, so he couldn’t tell you how it tasted.
Amar’e Stoudemire’s recovery routine: a bath of red wine. Not a sip of it.

Amar’e Stoudemire described a striking spa routine during Knicks training camp in 2014: soaking in a mixture of red wine and water, then having a ninety-minute massage. His wife had introduced him to the idea, and he said he had been doing it for months. Asked whether the wine itself was any good, he could not offer a tasting note: he had never tasted it.
A bathtub full of red wine
Loyola double-teamed Curry all game in 2008: zero points. Davidson still won by 30.
The one night Steph scored 0: two defenders stuck to him, and his teammates won by 30.

Stephen Curry finished a 2008 Davidson game without scoring and still received a standing ovation. Loyola assigned two defenders to shadow him, even without the ball. Curry often stood in a corner, taking both defenders with him and leaving his teammates to play four against three. He attempted just three shots. Davidson won 78–48, turning an extraordinary effort to stop one scorer into a comfortable team victory.
A standing ovation for zero points
2017: LeBron and the Cavs took the New York subway to beat traffic to the Garden.
LeBron on the subway. A guy nearby just wanted the cameras out of his face.

After a 2017 shootaround at Madison Square Garden, LeBron James and the Cavaliers took the subway back to their hotel. Kyle Korver explained their choice: a roughly six-minute train ride instead of a 45-minute bus trip. James filmed the unusual team commute, but the passenger beside him was unimpressed by the camera, asked him to stop and moved away. Even an NBA team had to navigate ordinary subway etiquette.
The subway passenger who wanted the camera away
During the 2011 lockout, Durant took a student up on a Twitter invite and played flag football.
KD played intramural flag football at Oklahoma State in 2011. A tweet set it up.

During the 2011 NBA lockout, Kevin Durant used Twitter to look for a flag-football game. Oklahoma State student George Overbey invited him, and Durant actually joined the game in Stillwater that night. The encounter acquired an unlikely second life two years later: Twitter included it in its stock-market flotation prospectus as an example of connections made through the service. A casual football invitation became material in a federal securities filing.
The pickup game that reached an SEC filing
Westbrook’s pregame PB&J: toasted wheat, Skippy, strawberry jelly, cut down the middle.
Russ took his pregame sandwich seriously. Toasted, Skippy, strawberry, cut straight. After a nap.

Russell Westbrook described a remarkably specific pregame routine on Jimmy Kimmel Live in 2015: an hour-long nap, then a peanut-butter-and-jelly sandwich made with toasted wheat bread, Skippy peanut butter and strawberry jelly, cut in half. He also called his parents. In a later interview, he again identified the nap and sandwich as part of his routine. The precise preparation was as memorable as the supposedly simple snack.
50 points to win the 2021 title, then 50 chicken minis at Chick-fil-A, live on Instagram.
Giannis celebrated his ring with a Chick-fil-A run. He ordered exactly 50, for his 50 points.

The morning after scoring 50 points in the game that clinched Milwaukee’s 2021 championship, Giannis Antetokounmpo took the trophy to a Chick-fil-A drive-through. Broadcasting on Instagram, he requested a 50-piece order of chicken minis and emphasized that the number must be exactly 50. He also ordered a drink mixed from Sprite and lemonade. Fans gathered around, bringing championship chants to an unusually public victory breakfast.
A championship celebration at the drive-through
Jokić was drafted during a Taco Bell commercial. TV missed his pick.
The future three-time MVP: 41st pick in 2014, announced while TV ran a Taco Bell ad.

When Denver selected Nikola Jokić with the 41st pick in the 2014 draft, American television viewers were watching a Taco Bell Quesarito commercial. His selection appeared in a small graphic beneath the advertisement. The awkward introduction became a lasting part of his basketball story. Asked about it years later, Jokić said he thought he had never eaten Taco Bell because of that draft-night moment.
A future MVP beneath a Taco Bell commercial
Luka heard Slovenian from courtside at a Lakers game. It was Kobe, talking to him.
Kobe surprised a young Luka Dončić by trash-talking him in Slovenian.

During a 2019 game against the Lakers, Luka Dončić heard someone courtside speaking to him in Slovenian. He turned around and found Kobe Bryant. Years later, Dončić recalled the encounter at a press conference, saying it was remarkable that Bryant even knew his name. A familiar language had delivered an unfamiliar courtside surprise, and the exchange remained vivid in his memory long afterward.
The Slovenian voice belonged to Kobe
Embiid says he learned his shot on YouTube, copying the form of ordinary shooters.
Joel Embiid started playing at 15. YouTube was his first shooting coach, he says.

Joel Embiid described an unconventional shooting education in a 2018 first-person essay. As a developing player in Florida, he kept losing shooting contests to teammate Michael Frazier II. He began searching YouTube for three-point shooting tutorials and studying ordinary people whose technique looked smooth. Embiid said he copied their form and practiced with Frazier for hours. His account makes anonymous online shooters part of an NBA star’s education.
His shooting teachers were strangers on YouTube
Bubble 2020: Jimmy Butler sold coffee from his hotel room. $20 a cup, cash only.
Big Face Coffee began as Jimmy Butler’s $20 hotel-room brew in the NBA bubble.

Inside the NBA’s 2020 bubble, Jimmy Butler noticed that players receiving their cash allowances had twenty-dollar bills. He began selling coffee for $20 a cup, cash only, with exact change required. His hotel-room venture became BigFace, a business he continued developing after the bubble. By 2022, its coffee was being served at the Miami Open tennis tournament. A peculiar temporary marketplace had helped launch a lasting side business.
Kawhi kept driving his old high school Chevy Tahoe long after his big contract.
Max money, same old Tahoe. Kawhi Leonard is not a car guy.

A 2016 profile found Kawhi Leonard still often driving the refurbished 1997 Chevrolet Tahoe he had used as a teenager. He called it the Gas Guzzler. The vehicle remained in his life even after a major NBA contract, and his explanation was practical: it worked and was already paid for. The memorable detail was the continuity between a teenage ride and the everyday transportation of an established star.
The superstar and his Gas Guzzler
A reporter stopped Klay on a New York street to ask about scaffolding. She had no idea who he was.
Three-time champ Klay Thompson gave a random street interview about scaffolding. Classic Klay.

A New York television reporter doing street interviews about scaffolding in 2017 happened to approach Klay Thompson. He offered earnest observations about checking overhead structures for safety problems, producing an unusually mundane interview with an NBA champion. Thompson later explained that the reporter had not initially recognized him, although the cameraman did. For a moment, a basketball celebrity’s role was simply to discuss the sidewalk above his head.
Draymond played in Michigan State’s 2011 spring football game. False start, then an incompletion.
Draymond Green, tight end? One spring football game at Michigan State. It went how you’d think.

Draymond Green made a brief appearance in Michigan State’s 2011 spring football game. His first involvement produced a false-start penalty. On the next play, he lined up wide and the pass went over his head, but the defender was penalized for holding him. Green had practiced with the team earlier that week. His crossover cameo produced no completed catch, but it gave the officials something to do.
A football cameo with two flags
Dame’s first real hoop: a milk crate his grandpa nailed to a telephone pole in Oakland.
Damian Lillard’s range started with a milk crate. Tiny target, no room for error.

Damian Lillard recalled that his childhood neighborhood used a curved oak-tree branch as a basketball hoop. When the city cut the tree down, his grandfather found a plastic milk crate, removed its bottom and nailed it to a telephone pole. A nearby streetlight extended their playing time. The replacement had a square opening and no flat backboard, so, in Lillard’s telling, it demanded shots that went straight through.
The tree hoop and the milk-crate replacement
Anthony Davis filed trademarks for “Fear the Brow.” The brow is staying.
Before his first NBA game, AD trademarked his eyebrow slogans. No razor deal could change his mind.

Before the 2012 NBA draft, Anthony Davis moved to protect phrases built around his distinctive unibrow, including “Fear the Brow” and “Raise the Brow.” He had resisted suggestions to shave it and explained that he wanted control over its commercial identity. Asked about a hypothetical razor endorsement, he said he would still keep it. His first professional branding story was already taking shape before his first NBA game.
Branding the brow before the draft
Paul George switched to No. 13 and gave his old No. 24 jerseys to his high school.
PG-13 used to be No. 24. Those jerseys went to his old high school.

When Paul George changed his Pacers number from 24 to 13 in 2014, he had met the deadline that exempted him from buying the remaining stock of his old jerseys. He bought them anyway. Instead of leaving the obsolete merchandise behind, he donated the jerseys to Knight High School, his alma mater in Palmdale. A rebranding decision that enabled the PG-13 nickname also sent a supply of NBA shirts back home.
The jersey change that supplied his old school
During the 2011 lockout, Blake Griffin interned at the comedy site Funny or Die.
Blake Griffin, comedy intern: he offered to fetch coffee at Funny or Die in 2011.

During the 2011 NBA lockout, reigning Rookie of the Year Blake Griffin took a short internship at Funny or Die. The planned three-day stint included meetings and a chance to learn about writing, filming and editing. Griffin told the Associated Press he wanted to learn how the operation worked and was willing to fetch coffee. At 22, he was the age of many interns, with a distinctly different résumé.
The NBA rookie who became a comedy intern
Chris Paul is a serious bowler. He won his own celebrity PBA event with pro Chris Barnes.
CP3 bowls for real: he hosts a PBA celebrity invitational and has won it.

At the 2017 CP3 PBA Celebrity Invitational, Chris Paul and professional bowler Chris Barnes faced Mookie Betts and Tommy Jones in the final. Paul missed a spare in the ninth frame, leaving the result in his partner’s hands. Barnes answered by striking out in the tenth, securing a 187–179 victory. In the charity event bearing his name, Paul got to experience a different kind of clutch performance from a teammate.
Chris Paul needed someone else to finish
Calvin Murphy was a champion baton twirler, and twirled at the nationals during his Rockets years.
Hall of Fame guard, 5′9″, and a championship baton twirler. Calvin Murphy.

Calvin Murphy had another competition to enter during his Rockets career: baton twirling. In 1977, he won the Texas men's state championship. He told TIME he had started at five, encouraged by six twirling aunts. That summer, the NBA guard was demonstrating routines for judges at the national championships in Denver.
Dave DeBusschere was an NBA head coach at 24, while playing, and pitched for the White Sox.
Player, coach and big-league pitcher at once: DeBusschere juggled all three in the 1960s.

At 24, Dave DeBusschere became the Pistons' player-coach while he was still pursuing professional baseball. That meant an NBA forward was also his teammates' boss and a pitcher in the White Sox organization. He kept pitching in the minors in 1965, then declined a late-season major-league call-up as basketball duties approached. By 1967, Detroit had also relieved him of coaching, leaving one job: playing basketball.
Detlef Schrempf played himself in three Parks and Recreation episodes.
Detlef Schrempf, sitcom star: three episodes of Parks and Rec as himself.

Parks and Recreation co-creator Michael Schur said the show first imagined a Larry Bird cameo, then turned to Detlef Schrempf. Schrempf was visiting Los Angeles regularly because his son attended UCLA. What began as one appearance became three episodes. Schrempf later explained that acting was not his ambition; he accepted appearances like these to draw attention to his charitable foundation. Pawnee got a basketball guest star with another purpose.
Pawnee called instead of Larry Bird
Danny Ainge played third base for the Toronto Blue Jays before the Celtics got him.
Boston had to win a court fight with the Blue Jays to get Danny Ainge to play basketball.

Danny Ainge's route to the Celtics ran through a courtroom. Boston drafted him in 1981 while he was under contract to baseball's Toronto Blue Jays. Ainge later said he had warned NBA teams that drafting him would waste their time. A jury upheld Toronto's contract claim, so Boston could not simply put him in uniform. The teams eventually negotiated his release, turning a two-sport tug-of-war into an NBA career.
The rookie signing that needed a jury
Charlie Ward won the Heisman as Florida State’s quarterback, then became a Knicks point guard.
A Heisman winner in the NBA: Charlie Ward picked hoops over the NFL.

Charlie Ward's college career produced an unusual wardrobe change. In 1993, the Florida State quarterback won the Heisman Trophy. He was also running the school's basketball offense, part of teams that reached three NCAA tournaments. When he turned professional in 1994, New York selected him in the NBA's first round. Football's most celebrated college award had ended up in the home of a Knicks point guard.
The Heisman winner in a Knicks jersey
Pat Connaughton pitched in the Orioles system and had the best vertical at his NBA combine.
Connaughton set an eighth-grade goal to dunk. He topped the 2015 combine in jumping.

Pat Connaughton says reading that Vince Carter first dunked in sixth grade gave him a more modest deadline: eighth grade. His father bought a weighted vest, and the young Connaughton trained on hills and ledges. Before eighth grade ended, he was dunking at five-foot-ten. Years later, he supplied an unusually emphatic sequel at the 2015 NBA combine: a 44-inch maximum vertical jump, the best mark that year.
After two NBA titles, J.R. Smith went to college to play golf at North Carolina A&T.
J.R. Smith, college golfer: he enrolled at NC A&T in his 30s and made the team.

J.R. Smith skipped college on his way to the NBA, then enrolled after his professional basketball career. His new team at North Carolina A&T played golf. In 2021, the veteran champion became a freshman student-athlete, learning college life while competing in a different sport. By the following spring, he had another distinction to add to the basketball trophies: the university's male academic athlete of the year, with a reported 4.0 GPA.
The freshman with two NBA rings
Jerry Lucas co-wrote “The Memory Book,” a bestseller about memory tricks.
Jerry Lucas could memorise almost anything, and wrote a bestseller teaching how.

Jerry Lucas had an unusual subject to teach beyond basketball: how to remember things. In 1974, he coauthored The Memory Book with memory specialist Harry Lorayne. The book built recall around mental pictures and associations; a contemporary review described turning Minnesota into a tiny soda in your imagination. The NBA rebounder was helping readers retrieve names, numbers and words, too.
Darrell Armstrong drank coffee before games and ate chocolate at halftime. It worked for him.
Darrell Armstrong ran on caffeine and candy. Sixth Man and Most Improved in the same season.

Darrell Armstrong told the Orlando Sentinel that late West Coast tipoffs were making him tired, so coach Chuck Daly suggested coffee before a Warriors game. Armstrong liked how that night went and kept the ritual. The 1999 profile described a remarkably sweet routine: seven lumps of sugar in his coffee and two Hershey's Kisses at halftime.
Before Grandmama, Converse pitched an ad with Bird and Magic building Larry Johnson in a lab.
Larry Johnson in a dress and a wig: the Grandmama ads made him a star.

Larry Johnson's famous Converse grandmother character followed a very different advertising concept. A 1994 SLAM profile described Larry Bird and Magic Johnson as laboratory scientists assembling the ideal player: Bird's first name, Magic's last name, and Larry Johnson emerging as the result. That campaign was shelved. Grandmama became the alternative, and Johnson told SLAM he had doubts before embracing the role. One of basketball's best-known commercial characters began as Plan B.
Anthony Mason shaved New York landmarks and slogans into his hair.
Mase’s haircuts were works of art. Literally: skylines in the fade.

Anthony Mason's Knicks haircuts could carry a miniature New York tribute. Barber Freddy Avila carved designs that included the Statue of Liberty and a city skyline beneath the team's name. The family connection outlasted those famous cuts: in a 2007 interview, Anthony Mason Jr. said he still used Cutty's, the same family barbershop as his father. His own variation was smaller: an M shaved into an eyebrow.
“Big Smooth”: Sam Perkins says the Smooth came from strolling into Lakers practice, late and calm.
Sam Perkins earned “Smooth” in LA. A Seattle broadcaster added the “Big.”

Sam Perkins says his nickname started with a near-miss at Lakers practice. Players had to be in a circle by 9:45 or pay a fine. His teammates saw him rush toward the locker room minutes beforehand and expected him to be late. Instead, he calmly walked back and arrived on time. Byron Scott teased him for looking smooth; Perkins recalled that Seattle broadcaster Kevin Calabro later supplied the Big.
Smooth enough to beat the fine
Ron Artest worked at Circuit City as a Bulls rookie. He wanted the employee discount.
Metta World Peace sold electronics after practice as a rookie. For the discount.

Metta World Peace says his first Bulls contract came with an unexpected side job: working at Circuit City. Then known as Ron Artest, he wanted something to do after practice and liked the employee discount. In his account, customers could buy electronics from an actual NBA rookie. He said the stint ended after Bulls executive Jerry Krause questioned it. Basketball practice and retail shifts briefly occupied the same schedule.
Lloyd Free legally changed his first name to World. All-World stuck.
World B. Free got his name from a playground dunk. Then he made it official.

World B. Free traced his unusual name to a Rucker Park dunk. In an interview, he recalled doing a 360-degree dunk in front of local nickname-giver Herb Smith, who started calling him All World. The crowd joined in. Free, originally named Lloyd, later made World his legal first name. The name on an NBA roster had begun as a playground reaction that he chose to keep.
Stevie Wonder named Darryl Dawkins “Chocolate Thunder.”
Darryl Dawkins named his dunks. Stevie Wonder named Darryl.

Darryl Dawkins credited a musician with one of basketball's most memorable nicknames. In interviews, he said Stevie Wonder came to games with someone describing the action and gave him the name Chocolate Thunder. Dawkins also recalled meeting Wonder in the 76ers' locker room. The label that sounded tailor-made for a powerful dunker had, in his telling, come from a fan famous for an entirely different kind of performance.
Kevin Love wore his dad’s vintage Beach Boys jacket into the arena.
Kevin Love’s tunnel fits came from his dad’s closet. Beach Boys gear included.

Kevin Love wore his dad's old Oregon jacket to a 2025 game. The UCLA alumnus recalled Erik Spoelstra asking, “Did you lose a bet?” Next came his father's Beach Boys jacket. Love's uncle Mike helped found the band, making both outfits tributes to his family.
Mike Conley won the 2020 HORSE tournament from his home court, over-the-backboard shot and all.
Mike Conley’s only NBA-run title: HORSE, 2020, played from his own driveway court.

Mike Conley won a televised basketball competition in April 2020 without sharing a court with his opponent. During the NBA shutdown, an eight-player HORSE tournament connected players remotely. Conley used his home court to outlast Zach LaVine in the final. His winning challenge was a shot from behind the basket that traveled over the backboard. The finish turned an at-home trick shot into the tournament's deciding play.
RJ Barrett’s godfather is Steve Nash. Nash supplied his baby crib.
Watching his godfather Steve Nash in the 2010 playoffs pushed RJ Barrett toward the NBA.

Steve Nash's connection to RJ Barrett started before basketball lessons: he gave the family a crib when RJ was born. Nash and RJ's father, Rowan, were close friends and Canada teammates, and the Barretts asked Nash to be godfather. Years later, RJ watched Nash's Suns face the Lakers in the 2010 conference finals. Barrett said that visit helped crystallize his ambition to play at that level himself.
Micheal Williams made 97 free throws in a row in 1993. Still the NBA record.
97 straight at the line. Micheal Williams owns the NBA’s longest free-throw streak.

Micheal Williams' free-throw streak survived an entire NBA offseason. He began the run in March 1993, finished that season without another miss, and resumed making them when the next season opened. By the time a shot finally failed on November 9, he had made 97 in succession. Both the miss before the run and the miss that ended it came against San Antonio: the same opponent, with a summer between.
A free-throw streak that crossed summer
Serge Ibaka lost a scarf argument with OG Anunoby, so he bought scarves for the whole team.
Serge Ibaka’s arena arrivals were fashion shows. Giant scarves, and gifts for teammates.

OG Anunoby claimed he had introduced Serge Ibaka to scarves on Ibaka's fashion show. Soon, both Raptors arrived at a game wearing enormous versions. Ibaka later told GQ his irritation was genuine. He also said he bought teammates scarves as a bonding gesture. A neckwear argument had become a team fashion story.
Dr. J took off from the free-throw line at the 1976 ABA dunk contest. Jordan copied it later.
1980 Finals: Dr. J went behind the backboard and came out the other side for a layup.
SGA swept MVP, the scoring title, the title and Finals MVP in 2025. One season.
The Clippers traded Shai to OKC for Paul George in 2019. OKC also got a pile of picks.
Moses predicted “fo’, fo’, fo’” for the 1983 playoffs. The Sixers went 12–1.
Moses Malone went straight from high school to the pros in 1974. Three MVPs later, fair call.
Dwight Howard won the 2008 dunk contest in a Superman cape.
Dwight Howard won three straight Defensive Player of the Year awards, 2009 to 2011.
Shaq named him “Flash.” Dwyane Wade won three titles in Miami.
“Havlicek stole the ball!” 1965, the most famous radio call in Celtics history.
John Havlicek was drafted by the Cleveland Browns as a receiver. He picked Boston and eight rings.
Game 7, 1970: Willis Reed limped out of the tunnel on a torn thigh muscle and hit his first two shots.
Jayson Tatum scored 51 in a 2023 Game 7, the most ever in a Game 7.
Tatum won it all in 2024, Boston’s 18th banner.
Dave Cowens took time off in 1976 and drove a taxi in Boston.
Dave Cowens was the 1973 MVP at 6′9″, undersized for a center and never outworked.
Wes Unseld started fast breaks with outlet passes thrown like fastballs.
Rick Barry shot free throws underhanded, granny style. Nearly 90% for his career.
The Iceman once scored 33 in a single quarter. Finger roll, no sweat.
Artis Gilmore won ABA Rookie of the Year and MVP in the same season, 1972.
The A-Train, 7′2″, retired as the NBA’s career leader in field-goal percentage.
Victor Wembanyama, the 2023 No. 1 pick, was a unanimous Rookie of the Year.
Wemby stands 7′4″ with an 8-foot wingspan and still shoots threes.
Game 7, 1970: with Reed hobbled, Walt Frazier went for 36 points and 19 assists.
Clyde got his name from a Bonnie and Clyde hat. The suits came after.
Clyde Drexler and Hakeem were Phi Slama Jama teammates in college. In 1995 they won a ring together.
Clyde the Glide was traded home to Houston in 1995 and won the title that June.
Bill Walton went to hundreds of Grateful Dead shows. He also won a title for Portland in 1977.
Zo blocked shots for the 2006 champion Heat three years after a kidney transplant.
Hal Greer played 15 seasons for one franchise and won the 1967 title with Wilt.
George McGinnis shared the 1975 ABA MVP with Julius Erving.
Big George won two ABA titles with Indiana before jumping to the NBA.
Spencer Haywood took the NBA to the Supreme Court and won the right to turn pro before college ended.
Every early-entry star owes Spencer Haywood. His 1971 court win opened the door.
Carmelo won Olympic gold in 2008, 2012 and 2016, plus a bronze in 2004.
Chris Bosh made 11 All-Star teams, in Toronto and Miami.
Bob Lanier wore size 22 shoes. One of them is on display at the Hall of Fame.
Bob Lanier was an eight-time All-Star with feet the size of a carry-on.
Sir Sid guarded everybody for Milwaukee. The NBA invented an award, and he won it twice.
The 1988 dunk contest, Dominique vs. Jordan, is still argued about.
They called Dominique Wilkins “The Human Highlight Film.” He earned it nightly.
McHale scored 56 in 1985, a Celtics record. Nine days later Bird scored 60.
Kevin McHale won Sixth Man of the Year twice before becoming a starter and a Hall of Famer.
Duke 1992: Grant Hill threw the full-court pass for Laettner’s famous buzzer-beater.
The NBA banned Connie Hawkins over a scandal he was never charged in. He sued and got in.
The Hawk won the ABA’s first MVP, toured with the Globetrotters, then starred in Phoenix.
“Penny” is from his grandmother saying “pretty.” Lil Penny, the puppet, was voiced by Chris Rock.
Penny Hardaway and Shaq took Orlando to the 1995 Finals in Penny’s second season.
1976 Finals, triple OT: Westphal called a timeout Phoenix didn’t have, on purpose, to set up a tying shot.
Paul Westphal’s illegal timeout trick forced a third overtime in the 1976 Finals.
Jordan’s childhood hero was David Thompson. MJ picked him to present his Hall of Fame entry.
Jermaine O’Neal went straight from high school to the NBA at 17 in 1996.
Jermaine O’Neal sat on Portland’s bench for four years, then became a six-time All-Star in Indiana.
Pistol Pete averaged 44.2 points a game at LSU, with no three-point line.
Pete Maravich scored 68 against the Knicks in 1977. Floppy socks and all.
Manu Ginóbili swatted a live bat out of the air during a 2009 Spurs game.
Ant won Olympic gold with Team USA in 2024.
Anthony Edwards went No. 1 in 2020 straight out of one season at Georgia.
When he retired, Lenny Wilkens had more coaching wins than anyone in NBA history.
Tony Parker won four rings with Duncan and Ginóbili in San Antonio.
Sam Jones won ten titles, second only to Bill Russell’s eleven.
Bill Sharman led the NBA in free-throw percentage seven times.
As Lakers coach, Bill Sharman ran the 1972 team that won 33 straight.
Heinsohn played, coached and called Celtics games for over six decades.
Kyrie hit the go-ahead three over Steph Curry in Game 7 of the 2016 Finals.
Kyrie Irving played “Uncle Drew” in ads, then in a movie. Old man, young handle.
Rudy Gobert has four Defensive Player of the Year awards, tied for the most ever.
The Stifle Tower: Rudy Gobert, 7′1″ with a 7′9″ wingspan.
Game 7, 1988 Finals: James Worthy had 36, 16 and 10. Big Game James.
James Worthy was the No. 1 pick in 1982, after winning a college title with Michael Jordan.
Joe Dumars was the 1989 Finals MVP. Later he built Detroit’s 2004 champs as GM.
Bird stole the ball in the 1987 playoffs and passed to Dennis Johnson, who laid it in to win.
Jo Jo White played 488 straight games for Boston. Ironman before it was cool.
In 1984 Bernard King scored 50 in back-to-back games, on back-to-back nights, in Texas.
Jaylen Brown was voted a vice-president of the players’ union at 24.
The “point forward” role was invented for Marques Johnson in Milwaukee.
The Chief won three rings in Boston and a fourth with Chicago at 43.
Tim Hardaway: one of the original Run TMC Warriors.
Mark Price made over 90% of his free throws for his career. Among the best ever.
Mark Price split traps before it was a thing. Cleveland’s four-time All-Star.
Marc Gasol went to high school in Memphis while big brother Pau played for the Grizzlies.
Gilbert Arenas was a second-round pick who became a three-time All-Star.
Donovan Mitchell scored 71 in a game in 2023.
Spida Mitchell’s dad worked for the New York Mets. Donovan grew up around baseball.
Devin Booker scored 70 at Boston in 2017. He was 20.
Booker won a three-point contest and Olympic gold, and reached the Finals in 2021.
Alex English, the 1980s’ top scorer, published books of poetry.
Alex English scored more points than anyone in the 1980s. Not Bird, not Magic.
Earl the Pearl spun past defenders before spin moves had names.
Gail Goodrich led the 1972 Lakers in scoring. They won 33 straight and the title.
Gail Goodrich won two NCAA titles at UCLA before his NBA ring.
Jack Sikma led the league in free-throw percentage, as a center.
Michael Cooper was the 1987 Defensive Player of the Year off the bench.
Coop-a-loop: Magic lobs, Michael Cooper finishes. Five Showtime titles.
Adrian Dantley won two scoring titles at 6′5″, mostly from the post.
They called Dražen Petrović “Mozart.” He once scored 112 in a European game.
Dražen Petrović made the All-NBA third team in 1993. He’s in the Hall of Fame.
Arvydas Sabonis was drafted in 1986 but didn’t join Portland until 1995, at 30.
Sabonis won Olympic gold for the Soviet Union in 1988. His son Domantas plays in the NBA.
Domantas Sabonis was born in Portland while his dad Arvydas played for the Blazers.
Domas Sabonis has led the NBA in rebounding. Dad was a Hall of Fame center.
Karl-Anthony Towns won the 2022 three-point contest. A center.
KAT was the No. 1 pick in 2015 and Rookie of the Year.
Tyrese Haliburton hit game-winners all through the 2025 playoffs on the way to the Finals.
Jalen Brunson’s dad, Rick, also played for the Knicks.
Brunson was a second-round pick who became the Knicks’ captain.
Tyson Chandler won a title with Dallas in 2011 and DPOY with the Knicks in 2012.
Tyson Chandler went straight from high school to the NBA as the No. 2 pick in 2001.
Starbury sold a $15 sneaker so kids could afford a signature shoe.
Iguodala won four rings with Golden State, mostly as a sixth man.
Vlade Divac was among the first Europeans to star in the NBA. He’s in the Hall of Fame.
Bill Bradley was a Rhodes Scholar, won two titles with the Knicks, then served 18 years in the Senate.
Senator Bill Bradley, D-New Jersey, used to set screens for Walt Frazier.
Maurice Stokes was paralyzed after a 1958 head injury. Teammate Jack Twyman became his guardian.
Jack Twyman was the second NBA player to average 30 in a season, in 1960.
Jerry Sloan coached the Jazz for 23 seasons. Same team the whole time.
Ja Morant was the 2020 Rookie of the Year and 2022 Most Improved Player.
Ja Morant came from Murray State, a small school, and went No. 2 overall.
Rip Hamilton wore a clear face mask after breaking his nose. He kept it for years.
Rip Hamilton ran defenders through screens all night for Detroit’s 2004 champs.
Dan Majerle went from Central Michigan to three All-Star games.
Kyle Lowry is the Raptors’ all-time assists leader.
Trae Young took the Hawks to the 2021 conference finals in his third season.
Rajon Rondo scored 44 against Miami in a 2012 conference finals game.
Al Horford’s dad, Tito, also played in the NBA.
Jrue Holiday won titles with Milwaukee in 2021 and Boston in 2024.
Jrue Holiday donated the rest of his 2020 salary to social-justice causes.
Bill Laimbeer won two titles with Detroit and later three WNBA titles as a coach.
Ralph Sampson was college player of the year three times at Virginia.
Ralph Sampson and Hakeem were the original Twin Towers in Houston.
Wayne Embry won a title as a player in Boston in 1968, then broke barriers in the front office.
